vignette: ### Clinical Vignette for Mr. Kaito Tavita Mr. Kaito Tavita, a 63-year-old Oceania man married to his lifelong partner and working as a publisher in a bustling office in the city, has been experiencing significant distress following a man-made disaster that occurred six months ago. The event, which involved an explosion at a nearby industrial plant, left Kaito deeply traumatized. Since then, he has found it increasingly difficult to navigate daily life. Kaito's memories of the event are vivid and detailed; every time he closes his eyes, the scene replays with such clarity that he often wakes up from nightmares sweating and trembling. These nightmares leave him feeling on guard even inside his own home. His wife has noticed that he constantly scans their surroundings for signs of threat, always sitting with his back against a wall to ensure he can see everything happening around him. Kaito had come to believe that by staying vigilant, he could prevent another disaster from occurring or at least be ready if it did. The memories are uncontrolled and intrusive; they force their way into Kaito’s mind when he does not want them to, often triggered by the smell of alcohol or discussions about the event. He has started avoiding social gatherings and seeing friends because the mere mention of the disaster can bring on a wave of intense fear and anxiety. The vividness of these memories is closely tied to his maladaptive strategies. Kaito's hyper-vigilance, both at home and in public spaces, stems from a deep-seated belief that he needs to be constantly aware of potential threats. This heightened state of alertness has led him to sit with his back against the wall at all times, feeling jumpy or easily startled by ordinary sounds that would not bother most people. His occupation as a publisher has also been affected; Kaito finds it difficult to concentrate on work when he is constantly scanning for potential dangers. The smell of cleaning products in the office sometimes triggers memories and causes him to feel overwhelmed, leading him to avoid certain areas or situations at work. Kaito’s wife notes that he often wakes up from nightmares feeling disoriented and anxious, which leads him to scan his environment again and again throughout the night. This cycle reinforces his belief that he needs to be hyper-vigilant even in safe spaces like their home. Recently, Kaito has started avoiding friends because any conversation about the disaster brings back vivid images of the explosion and the chaos that followed. He is certain that talking about it only exacerbates his symptoms and makes him feel more vulnerable. Consequently, he has become isolated from social support networks, which further intensifies his fear and anxiety. What frightens Kaito most is the prospect of another disaster occurring without warning, leaving him feeling powerless and unprepared. His maladaptive strategies have created a self-reinforcing cycle where each trigger leads to heightened vigilance, which in turn reinforces his negative appraisals about safety and control. He has reached out for help because he recognizes that these behaviors are taking over his life, but he is also afraid of what might happen if he stops being so vigilant. In summary, Kaito’s trauma symptoms have spiraled into a complex interplay of vivid memories, maladaptive strategies, and constant threat perception. This cycle has significantly impacted both his personal relationships and professional life, leading him to seek help in hopes of regaining control over his fears and finding ways to cope without isolation and hyper-vigilance.
